content.intro: Accessing Databases from C# is lesson 154 in APIs, Networking, and Database Integration. Integration code should isolate network or database calls, use parameters instead of string-built commands, validate external data, and define transaction boundaries.
content.why_it_matters: External systems fail and return untrusted data, so integration code needs timeouts, validation, and clear data boundaries. This lesson focuses on accessing databases from c# and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Database providers
items.text: Use explicit timeouts, parameterized database commands, small service boundaries, and validation for external results.

items.title: Parameterized commands
items.text: Treat a design pattern as a response to a recurring problem, not as a required layer. Explain the problem first, choose the smallest useful design, and keep refactoring protected by tests.

items.title: Data readers
items.text: For data readers, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to accessing databases from c#, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Transactions
items.text: Treat HTTP and database responses as untrusted boundaries. Set timeouts, check status codes, parameterize SQL, validate deserialized results, and make transaction scope and disposal explicit.

items.title: Async database operations
items.text: Await I/O-bound tasks, pass cancellation tokens across boundaries, and protect shared mutable state explicitly.

items.title: Resource cleanup
items.text: Use explicit paths and scoped resource disposal; test missing files, permission failures, and partial data.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates accessing databases from c#. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates accessing databases from c# rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for accessing databases from c# before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
